scene_start: Afternoon on Polmarren harbour. Old Jack is mending nets when Sam, down from London, stops to say hello.
beats: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot.
Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own.
Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Alright Jack, that looks like some proper heavy-duty work. How do you actually get those knots to stay tight without the whole thing unraveling? It’s a bit more complex than just patching up a bug in some code, isn't it?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what you're blathering on about with that code business, lad, but a knot is just a knot if you've got the steady hands for it. I learned to weave these fine meshes back when I was a nipper on the trawlers heading up to the Iceland banks. If you don't pull the twine true, the whole net'll slip right through your fingers when the heavy cod start pulling. You're a long way from the city, aren't you?

speaker: minh
text: Yeah, I'm a long way from the city, just taking a bit of leave to clear my head. That Iceland trip sounds intense, though—was the weather out there as mental as everyone says? I can't imagine trying to do any precision work with waves smashing into the boat like that.

speaker: lao
text: It weren't just mental, boy, it was a proper fight for your life when the grey swells came rolling in. I remember one night off the banks when the wind howled like a banshee and the deck was slick with ice and brine. You don't think about precision then, you just hold on tight and pray the hull holds steady against the swell. You've got a quiet look about you, lad, like you're carrying something heavy in your mind.

speaker: minh
text: You've got a sharp eye, Jack, but I'm alright, just trying to decompress from the London grind. It’s a bit different from dodging grey swells, I suppose. What kind of gear do you use to keep the boat steady when the weather gets that bad?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: We rely on the heavy anchors and the weight of the keel to keep us from being tossed like a cork, lad. But a boat's only as good as the man steering it through the dark. It's a lonely thing, being out there with nothing but the sound of the waves, so I reckon you're looking for a bit of that quiet yourself. Why'd you come all this way to Polmarren on your own, then?

speaker: minh
text: I'm just on a bit of leave, Jack, needed to get away from the constant notifications and the noise for a bit. It's a lot easier to think clearly when there's no signal and just the sound of the sea. Do you find the solitude out on the water helps you clear your head, or does it just get too quiet?

speaker: lao
text: The silence out there is a heavy thing, lad, but it's better than the noise of a crowded pub in a town. I used to find peace in it when my Mary was still with me, though it gets a bit too quiet now that she's gone. Sometimes I just watch the tide turn and think on the things I should've said when I had the chance. It's a strange thing, seeking out the emptiness when you're feeling low.

speaker: minh
text: I hear you, Jack; sometimes the quiet is the only thing that actually lets you process everything. It's a bit like when a system crashes and you're just sitting there in the dark waiting for the reboot. Do you spend most of your time out there on the water these days, or do you prefer staying closer to the harbour?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know a word about systems crashing or reboots, boy, so don't be wasting your breath on me. These days I mostly stay close to the harbour, just watching the tide and mending what's broken. My old bones aren't what they were when I was hauling nets in the North Sea, and I've got enough to do here tending to my gear. You've a peculiar way of speaking, lad, but you seem like a decent enough sort to sit and have a moment with.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Cheers, Jack, I appreciate that. It’s actually quite nice to just sit here and not have to be "on" for anyone. Do you reckon you'll be heading out on the boat at all tomorrow morning?

speaker: lao
text: I might head out for a bit of jigging if the swell stays low, but I'll likely stay on the quay mending these nets. It's a fine morning for it, though the wind's got a bit of a nip in it from the east. You've a look about you like you're searching for something more than just a bit of peace, lad. I wonder what kind of life they lead up there in London that makes a man run for the sea.

speaker: minh
text: It's just a lot of fast-paced nonsense, Jack, constant pressure to deliver results and stay connected 24/7. It's less about searching for something and more about just trying to find a bit of stability again. What's the best kind of bait to use if you're going to try that jigging tomorrow?

speaker: lao
text: If you're looking to catch something decent, you can't go wrong with a bit of fresh lugworm or some well-cut squid, lad. I remember my grandson Tommy once tried to use bits of bread he'd dropped, and we didn't catch a single thing but a bit of seaweed. You get the best results when the bait's fresh out of the bucket and smells of the salt. You're a strange lad, always talking in riddles, but I reckon you'll find your footing soon enough if you just sit still for a bit.

speaker: minh
text: Haha, bread? Tommy's a legend, that one. I'll definitely keep the lugworm tip in mind if I decide to try my luck. Thanks for the advice, Jack, it's been proper good chatting with you.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, Tommy's a handful, but he's got a good heart. It's been a fine talk, lad, and you're welcome to sit here a while if the shade suits you. I'll be here until the light fails, just working through this tear in the mesh. Mind you don't trip on those loose ropes on your way back up the slipway.

speaker: minh
text: Cheers, Jack, I'll definitely watch my step. I think I'll just hang about for a bit and enjoy the view. Any chance you've got a spare bit of twine I could look at, just to see how the weave works?

speaker: lao
text: I suppose I could let you have a look at a bit of the leftover twine, lad, though it's a messy business for hands not used to the work. I remember when my own father first sat me down on the edge of the pier to teach me the twist of a knot, and my fingers were as clumsy as a landed monkfish. Just be careful not to tangle it up too much or I'll be spending all evening untying your knots. You're a curious one, sitting there watching an old man work like it's something worth seeing.

summary: Sam, a man from London who works with computer code, visits Polmarren harbour to seek solitude from his fast-paced city life. He speaks with Jack, an elderly net mender who learned his craft on Iceland trawlers and has been widowed since the passing of his wife, Mary.

scene_start: Next morning, still dark, Sam goes out with Old Jack in his small boat.
beats: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out.
Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons.
They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Steady on now, lad, don't you be looking at the horizon if it makes your stomach turn like a tossed mackerel. Just keep your eyes on the gunwale and breathe deep the salt air, same as I did when I first went out on the trawlers at fourteen. It gets easier once you find your sea legs, but for now, just lean into the swell and let the boat do the work. There's no use fighting the Atlantic when she's decided to dance.

speaker: minh
text: Cheers, Jack, I'm trying, but this swell is properly mental. It's a bit like trying to debug a massive spaghetti code mess where everything's moving at once. Is it always this choppy out here before the sun even comes up?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what that code business is meant to be, lad, so don't go confusing me with your city talk. She's always a bit restless before the light breaks, especially when the wind's been blowing from the north all night. I mind my first time out on a big trawler when I was only fourteen, and I spent half the trip praying to the saints just to keep my breakfast down. It's a heavy sea this morning, but she'll settle once the sun gets some grip on the water.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, my bad, I'll dial back the tech talk. It's just a bit much, honestly, feeling like I'm being tossed around in a washing machine. What kind of gear do you use to keep track of where you're heading in this darkness?

speaker: lao
text: We use the compass and the stars if the clouds break, but mostly we just know these waters by the feel of the swell against the hull. I remember my first time out on the deep trawlers when I was only fourteen, and I spent more time staring at the compass needle than I did at the actual sea. You learn the landmarks and the depth by heart, or the sea will have you lost before you can say your prayers. Just hold onto the rail and trust the boat, lad.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That's proper impressive, just knowing the way by feel without any GPS or sat-nav. I actually wanted to film some of this, but my phone's completely dead, which is a massive L. So, how do the tides and the seasons change where you decide to drop the nets?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what a phone or an L is, lad, so leave that nonsense to the folk in London. We watch the moon and the way the currents pull against the cliffs to know where the fish be running. In the winter, the swell gets a hard edge to it that'll shake the teeth right out of your head, much like the storms I saw back in '87. You learn to read the water like a book, or you'll find yourself in a bad way.

speaker: minh
text: Sorry, Jack, I'll stop with the slang. It's mad that you can read the water like a book just by watching the currents. Do you have to look for specific types of seaweed or something to know if the ground below us is right for the nets?

speaker: lao
text: It's more about the color of the water and the way the kelp drifts in the current, lad. I mind my first time out on the big trawlers when I was but fourteen, and I spent hours watching the bottom-trawlers drag through the seabed to see how the weed came up. You look for the certain patches of wrack that tell you the ground is soft enough for the gear to settle without snagging. It's a feeling in your bones as much as it is a sight for your eyes.

speaker: minh
text: That's mental, it's like you've got a built-in sensor for the seabed. I wish I could've captured that on video, but my phone's totally bricked. When you're looking for those patches of wrack, is it harder to spot when the water is this dark?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: It's harder, aye, but you learn to spot the shadows even in the blackest night. Hold steady now, lad, because the net's pulling heavy and there's something strange thrashing in the mesh. Lord above, look at the size of that thing with the silver scales and the jagged fins. I've never seen a fish quite like it in all my years out on the deep water.

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, Jack, that thing is massive! It looks like something straight out of a sci-fi film, I'm gutted my phone's dead because I'd love to get a clip of that. Is it a type of monkfish or something even rarer?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea about no sci-fi films, lad, so don't be filling my head with such nonsense. It looks more like a great conger eel or perhaps a rogue monkfish, but it's a fine sight nonetheless. Seeing a beast like that brings me right back to being fourteen years old on those Iceland trawlers, staring at something equally strange in the dark. Just keep your hands clear of the mesh until I get the knife ready to cut it loose.

speaker: minh
text: Right, I'll keep my hands back, don't worry. It's properly surreal seeing something that looks so prehistoric just popping out of the net like that. Does a catch like this happen often, or is it a once-in-a-lifetime thing?

speaker: lao
text: A catch like that is a rare blessing, lad, and I've not seen nothing like it since my first week out on the deep trawlers at fourteen. I remember pulling up a massive wreck of a crab then, and my heart was thumping against my ribs like a trapped bird. It's a strange thing to see such a beast surfacing when the sun hasn't even thought of rising. We'll be talking about this one down at the pub when we get back to the harbour.

speaker: minh
text: I bet the lads at the pub will lose their minds when you tell them. It's just a shame I can't show them myself since my phone's completely dead. What's the plan once we've got it sorted, do we head straight back or do you try to keep fishing?

speaker: lao
text: We'll head straight back to the quay once we've got this beauty stowed, for a catch like this needs to be iced quick. I've no use for more nets today after seeing something so strange rise from the deep. It takes me right back to being fourteen years old on those Iceland trawlers, wondering if the sea was hiding monsters under every wave. We'll get this in and then I'll find a bit of peace with a pint while the village wakes up.

speaker: minh
text: Sounds like a plan, Jack, a pint sounds proper decent right now. It's mad how one weird catch can completely change the vibe of the whole morning. Is there a specific place in the village where everyone gathers to talk about the day's haul?

summary: Sam and Jack head out on a boat in the dark to fish, where they pull up a massive, unidentified silver fish in the nets. Sam reveals he is from the city and uses tech slang, while Jack shares that he began working on deep-sea trawlers in Iceland when he was fourteen.

scene_start: Midday on the quay, Old Jack sells his catch and Sam lends a hand.
goal: A morning at the fish stall.
beats: A customer haggles hard over the price.
Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off.
The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A customer haggles hard over the price. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That bloke's really rinsing you on the price, Jack, it's a joke. Is he always this much of a nightmare to deal with? I feel like he's basically trying to exploit a bug in your pricing system.

speaker: lao
text: Don't you worry none about that, lad, for that's just how Arthur's been since his father passed. He's a tight-fisted soul, always trying to squeeze a copper out of a stone, but he's paid for his mackerel since before you were born. I've known him forty years and he's never once paid a fair price to a man with honest hands. Just keep your eyes on the crates and don't let his haggling get under your skin.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, I'll just keep my head down and watch the stock then. It's a bit of a grind, though, isn't it? Do you ever think about, I don't know, getting the word out online to avoid the middleman entirely?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't the foggiest what you're on about with that online talk, boy, as I can barely work a mobile phone. We've always done things by the quay, selling straight to the folk who need it, like young Billy who takes the crabs for his mother. If you want to reach people, you just shout loud enough or wait for the morning tide to bring the customers. It's better to look a man in the eye when you're trading than to be chasing ghosts in a machine.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, Jack, there's something proper real about doing it face-to-face. It's just that the "ghosts in the machine" could basically be your entire customer base if you hooked them properly. What kind of fish do people usually come looking for first thing in the morning?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Most folk come sniffing 'round for the fresh mackerel or maybe some pilchards if the season's right. You'll see Mrs. Tregenza come by first, always looking for the best sprats to make her soup, or young Tomkins looking for crab. Here, you've gone and handed me a tenner when it was only a fiver, you silly lad. Ha, don't look so worried, I'll keep your extra coin safe for when you find your wits again.

speaker: minh
text: My bad, Jack, I'm clearly running on low battery today. It's just a bit of a system error, I promise. Do you have a regular list of these people, like a set schedule of who shows up for what?

speaker: lao
text: I don't use no lists or schedules, lad, because you just have to know the rhythm of the village. You'll see Old Man Penhaligon come by when the tide is turning, always looking for a bit of cod to fry up. Then there's little Sarah who comes round with her mother once the sun's high, looking for the smallest silver fish for her supper. You learn the faces and the needs of the folk round here, and that's all the planning a man ever needs.

speaker: minh
text: That's actually pretty impressive, it's like you've got a built-in algorithm for the whole village. I was thinking of suggesting a website or something to automate the orders, but I don't want to sound like a total prat. Does the rhythm of it change much when the weather gets properly mental?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't the faintest what an algorithm is, boy, so stop using them strange words. When the weather turns foul and the wind howls like a banshee, the quay goes quiet as a grave and nobody comes looking for fish. I remember the Great Storm of eighty-seven when the sea rose up and nearly took the pier right out from under us. On days like that, we just batten down the hatches and wait for the swell to die down before we even think of the nets.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, eighty-seven sounds absolutely mental, I can't even imagine the sea being that much of a nightmare. Wait, did that lady just say what I think she said? Jack, please tell me she's just taking the piss about us being related.

speaker: lao
text: That was just Mrs. Tregenza having a bit of a laugh, lad, for she's always been a bit of a joker with the newcomers. She's got a sharp tongue, but she doesn't mean a word of it about you being kin to my Mary. She likely saw your bright eyes and thought you looked a bit like my grandson Tommy when he's being cheeky. Don't you take it to heart, for she's just teasing a city boy to see if he'll blush.

speaker: minh
text: Safe, that's a relief, I was about to have a proper panic attack. She's got a bit of a savage sense of humour, hasn't she? Do you think people around here would be open to something like a pre-order system, or would that be way too much of a leap?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what a pre-order is, boy, but nobody here is going to tell them what to do before they've seen the silver in the bucket. You'll find folks like Silas the blacksmith won't be wanting any fancy business, as he just shows up when his belly's rumbling. Then there's Widow Poldark, who's been coming for her single fillet every Tuesday since my Mary passed. They like to see the fish themselves to know it's fresh from the salt, and they won't be changing that for nothing.

speaker: minh
text: That makes sense, people want to see the actual hardware before they buy it, I guess. It sounds like everyone's got their own set routine that's hard to break. Does anyone ever come in from the bigger towns nearby to buy your catch, or is it strictly local?

speaker: lao
text: We get a few folks from Penzance coming down on the bus, but mostly it's the local lot who keep us going. You'll see young Arthur from the bakery coming by for his morning pilchards, or even the doctor's wife looking for a bit of crab. Sometimes a chef from a fancy place in Falmouth will drive up, but they're rare as hen's teeth and always looking for the biggest catch. It's a small circle, lad, but it's a circle that's kept this village alive for generations.

speaker: minh
text: It's a pretty tight-knit loop you've got going here, isn't it? A chef from Falmouth sounds like a massive upgrade, though, like a premium tier client or something. Do they ever try to haggle for bulk orders, or do they just pay whatever you ask for the top-shelf stuff?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what a premium tier is, lad, so you'll have to speak plain English for an old man. Those Falmouth chefs are a different breed, wanting the finest turbot and always trying to talk me down to a pittance. They'll come in with their shiny cars and their fancy talk, acting like they've never seen a fish before they've seen it. I remember one fellow once tried to tell me my crab wasn't fresh enough, even though I'd pulled it from the water only an hour before.

summary: Sam assists Jack with selling fish on the quay and mistakenly hands him a ten-pound note instead of five. Jack explains his long-standing local trade patterns and reveals that he is a widower whose grandson is named Tommy.

scene_start: Evening, a storm is coming in; Sam runs down to help Jack haul the boat up the slipway.
beats: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips.
Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987.
The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Easy now, lad, grab that line 'fore the swell takes her! That rope's gone slack and she's sliding right off the timber. It’s just like that night back in eighty-seven when the wind came screaming out of nowhere and took the Mary-Ann with her. Keep your footing on that wet stone or you'll be in the drink with the rest of us.

speaker: minh
text: Right, I've got it, Jack! This is mental, the swell is massive compared to anything I've seen back home. Is the weather always this unpredictable around here, or is this a proper outlier?

speaker: lao
text: The sea don't care much for your city words, boy, she just does what she pleases. This swell's got a nasty bit of temper to it, much like the gale that took young Billy from under me in eighty-seven. I still see his face in the white foam when the wind howls through the eaves of the cottage. Best get her tied tight and get off the slipway 'fore the spray blinds you.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, that's heavy, Jack. I've never actually seen a storm this intense in real life—it's like my brain's buffering trying to process all this chaos. Is there a specific spot in the village where it's safer to wait out a gale like this?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what you're babbling about with that buffering business, lad, so just keep your wits about you. You best get yourself down to the old inn, the Ship Inn, and stay well away from the quay. I'll head up to my cottage to see if I can't get the shutters bolted against the wind. It's a fierce one coming, and I've seen enough trouble on these rocks for ten lifetimes.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: The Ship Inn sounds like a plan, Jack. You mentioned '87 before—was that the same massive storm everyone in London was talking about, or was that something different? It feels like the whole sky is about to glitch out.

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about your glitches or what they say in London, lad, but that storm in eighty-seven was a beast unlike any other. The sky turned a bruised purple and the wind tore the very breath from your lungs. It was that night the sea claimed young Billy, just as we were pulling in the last of the nets near the cliffs. Now move along to the inn 'fore the heavens truly break.

speaker: minh
text: Right, I'm off, Jack. It's actually a bit terrifying, but seeing the sky turn that colour is mental—properly surreal. Do you live right on the edge of the cliffs, or is your cottage tucked further back from the spray?

speaker: lao
text: My cottage sits back a fair bit, tucked behind the stone wall where the wind can't bite quite so hard. It’s a sturdy little place, built well enough to keep the damp out when the spray flies high. I sat in that very kitchen when the eighty-seven gale rattled the windowpanes and I sat alone thinking of Billy. Get yourself to the inn now, lad, and don't be looking back at the sea.

speaker: minh
text: Safe, Jack, I'm heading off. It’s actually kind of wild seeing the ocean go this hard, even if it is a bit terrifying. Does the inn have a fireplace where I can sit and wait for this to pass?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
(Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: The Ship Inn has a hearth big enough to roast a whole pig, so you'll find plenty of warmth there. Come on then, the rain's turning to sleet and my old bones are feeling the damp. We'll head up to my place instead where I've got a bit of peat on the fire and a dry roof. I'll put the kettle on once we've got the door shut against this blow.

speaker: minh
text: That's sound, Jack, thanks a lot. I'm not gonna lie, my heart's absolutely racing because I've never actually experienced a proper storm like this before. Is the peat fire something you use often to keep the house warm?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: Aye, a bit of peat goes a long way when the wind is howling through the thatch, lad. I remember my Mary used to keep the embers glowing all night so the house wouldn't feel so empty once she passed. It's a comfort to have a steady flame when the darkness settles in thick over the cove. Come on now, watch your step on those cobbles 'fore you slip.

speaker: minh
text: I'm watching my step, I swear! This whole thing is actually peak adrenaline, like a high-res simulation but way more intense. Was Mary the one who taught you how to manage the peat fire, or did you learn that yourself?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: I don't know what you mean by a simulation, boy, I only know the feel of real smoke in me eyes. Mary was the one who kept the hearth tidy, always making sure the peat was laid just right for a long night. I learned to tend it myself after she went, though it's a hard thing to do alone in a quiet house. Now move your feet, the wind is picking up and the sea is turning white.

speaker: minh
text: Got it, I'm moving! Honestly, the way the sea is turning white is absolutely mental, it's like everything is crashing at once. Do you find it's easier to sleep when the wind is this loud, or does it just make the house feel even quieter?

speaker: lao
text: The wind don't help a man sleep, lad, it only makes the silence in the house feel heavier. When the gale howls like this, I can't help but remember the sound of the waves crashing on the rocks back in eighty-seven. It's a lonely sort of noise that makes you think of all the ones the sea's taken from us. Come on, let's get inside 'fore the rain starts lashing us proper.

speaker: minh
text: I'm right behind you, Jack. The noise is actually insane, it's like the whole world is being overwritten by this massive roar. Do you have any old photos or stuff around the house from before the storm in eighty-seven?

summary: Sam and Jack secure a boat on the slipway before deciding to seek shelter at Jack's cottage. Jack reveals that he lost a boy named Billy and his wife, Mary, to the sea and storms in 1887.

scene_start: Stormy night, Sam stays at Jack's cottage; they sit by the fire.
beats: Jack toasts kippers for Sam.
Sam finally tells the truth about burnout and the breakup.
Jack talks about his late wife.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack toasts kippers for Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That sounds proper lovely, Jack, definitely beats the overpriced takeout I usually grab in London. Is there a specific way you prep them, or is it just a quick heat up? I'm absolutely starving after that madness on the boat.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: Sit yourself down by the hearth, lad, and I'll get some crusty bread and some leftover pilchard stew going for you. You can't rush a good meal like you rush everything else in that city of yours. I remember my old mate Silas, a man who always tried to eat his supper while the pot was still boiling on the stove. He ended up burning his tongue so bad he couldn't taste the salt in the sea for a week, and a man needs his senses when the waves get high.

speaker: minh
text: Cheers, Jack, that sounds like a proper lifesaver right now. Honestly, my brain feels like it's constantly running too many background processes, so I think I forgot how to actually slow down. It's a bit of a system crash, if I'm being real.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: I don't know much about your systems or your crashes, boy, but I do know about a man named Arthur who used to work the winch on the Star of Cornwall. He used to try and pull the nets in too fast, thinking he could beat the tide if he just worked harder and quicker. One night the gear jammed because he'd pushed it too far, and he spent three days sitting on a crate just watching the tide come in, learning how to sit still. You ought to do the same and just let the stew warm your bones.

speaker: minh
text: I guess Arthur had the right idea, because I've been pushing my own gears way too hard lately. It’s not just the work, really; my girlfriend and I split up a few weeks ago, and it feels like my whole life's logic has just broken. I didn't think I'd be telling a stranger this, but it's a lot to process.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam finally tells the truth about burnout and the breakup. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
(Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: It's a heavy weight to carry, lad, and it'll pull you down deep if you don't find a way to float. My old friend Elias lost his sweetheart to a fever in a small cove near Penzance, and he spent months staring at the horizon like he'd forgotten how to speak. He spent a whole season mending nothing but old, torn nets, just letting the rhythm of the needle and thread quiet his mind until he could stand upright again. You just take it one stitch at a time, and soon enough the pattern will start to make sense once more.

speaker: minh
text: That's actually a really beautiful way of looking at it, Jack, thanks for saying that. I feel like I've just been stuck in a loop, trying to debug a problem that I can't even see. Do you think it ever actually gets easier, or do you just get better at managing the errors?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: you have repeated these ideas too often: eighty seven. Talk about something else this turn, be more concrete.)
text: I don't know nothing about your loops or your errors, boy, but I remember an old skipper named Barnaby who lost his main rudder in a swell off the Lizard. It didn't get any less choppy, but he learned exactly how much muscle to put into the wood to keep from capsizing. You just learn how to hold the oar, lad, and the water will eventually settle.

speaker: minh
text: That's a heavy analogy, Jack, but I think I get what you're saying about just keeping a steady heading. It's just hard when it feels like the whole sea is crashing over you at once, you know? I feel like I've been trying to steer with a broken rudder for months.

speaker: lao
text: I remember a lad from the village, young Tomkins, who went out in a skiff with a cracked hull during a gale. He spent the whole night bailing water with a small tin bucket, certain he was going to sink to the bottom of the Atlantic. He didn't fix the crack right then, he just kept that bucket moving until the sun came up and the sea turned to glass. Once the sun was up, he could see the damage clearly and patch it properly with a bit of pitch and wood.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack talks about his late wife. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That makes sense, I guess I've just been trying to patch the cracks while the storm is still raging. I think I need to wait for the sun to come up before I can even figure out where the damage is. It's just... it's been so lonely, being stuck in my own head like this.

speaker: lao
text: Loneliness is a quiet tide that can pull a man out far from the shore if he isn't careful, lad. I remember my Mary when she first came to the cottage, and there were nights when the wind howled so loud in the chimney it felt like the house was empty even when she sat right beside me. We'd just sit there in the dark, listening to the gale, and she'd reach out and take my hand so I knew I wasn't drifting alone in the black. You just have to find someone to hold the lamp for you while the wind blows.

speaker: minh
text: That's a proper heavy thought, Jack, and it hits a bit close to home. I think I've spent so long staring at screens and code that I've forgotten how to actually connect with anyone. It’s weird, but being here, just sitting by your fire, makes the silence feel a bit less daunting.

speaker: lao
text: I'm glad the fire's doing its work, lad, for a warm hearth is a fine thing for a weary soul. There was an old man in Polmarren, Silas the Weaver, who used to sit on the quay every evening just watching the boats come in. speaker: minh
text: I think I've been too busy trying to optimize everything that I've completely lost my connection to the real world. It's like I've been living in a sandbox mode, totally isolated from anything that actually matters. I really needed to hear that, Jack, thank you.

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what a sandbox is, boy, but I remember a man named Caleb who tried to build a stone wall on the cliffside without ever touching the earth. He spent all his days drawing plans in the sand, thinking he could make a wall that didn't need to fight the wind or the salt. One night the tide came in and swept his drawings clean away, leaving him standing there with nothing but his own two bare feet on the wet rocks. He had to learn to get his hands dirty in the real mud if he ever wanted to see a wall stand true.

speaker: minh
text: That's a massive reality check, Jack, and I think I've been drawing way too many plans in the sand lately. I've been so obsessed with the perfect architecture of my life that I forgot I actually have to live it. It's a bit of a wake-up call, honestly.

speaker: lao
text: It's a hard lesson to learn, lad, but a man can't live on drawings alone. I remember an old boatbuilder named Thomas who spent years trying to carve a hull so perfect it had no knots in the wood. He ended up with a vessel so brittle it split apart the first time a heavy swell hit it, whereas the rough, knotty oak boats always held fast. A bit of imperfection in the grain is what makes a thing strong enough to weather the actual sea.

summary: Sam and Jack sit by a fire in Jack's cottage while eating pilchard stew. Sam reveals that he lives in London and recently ended a relationship with his girlfriend.

scene_start: Morning after the storm, Jack's boat is holed; Sam watches him patch the hull.
beats: Jack shows Sam how to mix the tar for the patch.
Tommy runs down wanting to help and knocks over the tar pot.
Sam asks why Jack doesn't buy a new boat.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack shows Sam how to mix the tar for the patch. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Now, pay close attention, lad, 'cause if the mix is too thin, the sea'll find its way right through. You've got to stir that tar slow and steady with the pine resin until it's thick as treacle. I bought this old girl with the savings Mary set aside, so I'll be damned if I let a bit of rot sink her. Just keep your eyes on the consistency and don't let the fire get too hot.

speaker: minh
text: Got it, Jack, I'll keep an eye on the temperature so we don't burn the whole batch. It’s actually pretty therapeutic, seeing something get fixed step-by-step instead of just debugging lines of code. Is that resin stuff something you had to learn the hard way, or did someone teach you the recipe?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what a debug is, boy, so don't go using them strange words on me. My father taught me how to seal a hull when I was no older than your little Tommy. He used to say a man's boat is his life, and if you don't treat her right, she'll leave you to the sharks. We'll get this patch set, and then we'll see if we can get her back out on the swell.

speaker: minh
text: Sorry, Jack, my bad—basically just means fixing mistakes, but I'll stick to plain English. It's actually quite satisfying seeing this stuff thicken up and work in real-time. Did your dad use the same kind of pine resin back then, or has the process changed much since he taught you?

speaker: lao
text: It's the same old way my father used, lad, and it's worked for more generations than you've been breathing. We gather the resin from the woods just as we always have, for the sea don't care for new ways of doing things. I'll be using every penny of the savings Mary left me to make sure this hull is watertight again. Just keep that paddle moving so the mixture don't go cold on us.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Tommy runs down wanting to help and knocks over the tar pot. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: On it, Jack, I'm keeping it moving. It's weirdly calming to actually see the results of what I'm doing right in front of me. Wait, is that Tommy running down the path toward us?

speaker: lao
text: Aye, that's my Tommy alright, running like a terrier after a rabbit. He's probably come to see if we've finished up so he can go down to the quay and see the boats coming in. He's got his mother's eyes, that boy, and a spirit that's far too bright for a man as old and tired as me. Keep that mixture moving, lad, or he'll be here to find us sitting idle.

speaker: minh
text: He's a lively one, isn't he? I've got the paddle going, don't you worry. It's actually quite decent working with my hands like this, feels way more solid than just typing on a keyboard all day.

speaker: lao
text: It’s good for a man to feel the weight of a tool in his hand, lad, instead of just chasing shadows. I remember when I first took to the deep waters near Iceland, my hands were nothing but blisters and salt-sores from the ropes. This boat is a precious thing to me, bought with the very savings Mary worked so hard to keep tucked away. Now, stop your jawing and keep that paddle turning so the resin stays true.

speaker: minh
text: Right, sorry, I'm on it! I'm keeping a steady rhythm so the consistency stays perfect. It's actually pretty cool how much physical effort this takes compared to what I'm used to.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam asks why Jack doesn't buy a new boat. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Why should I go buying a shiny new boat when this one knows the currents of this cove like the back of my hand? A new vessel's got no soul in her, and she hasn't the history that Mary and I built together on these waters. I've seen many a man lose his shirt buying fancy gear only to find the sea doesn't respect a new hull any more than an old one. Just keep that rhythm steady, lad, for we've got much more work to do before the tide turns.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, Jack, there's a certain logic to sticking with what works instead of chasing the latest upgrade. Honestly, I'm actually starting to find this bit of manual labour pretty decent. How long do you reckon it'll take us to finish the whole hull before the tide does turn?

speaker: lao
text: If the weather holds and we don't let this mix go stone cold, we'll have the whole seam sealed by mid-morning. I remember a time off the coast of Iceland when a swell nearly took my arm clean off, and we had to patch a leak in the dark just to stay afloat. We've got about three hours before the tide starts its turn, so don't you go slowing down on me now. Keep that paddle moving, lad, and we'll have her ready for the swell.

speaker: minh
text: Three hours, right, I've got it. I'm keeping the pace up so we don't miss the window. It's mad to think you were patching leaks in the dark in Iceland, but I'm definitely feeling more in the zone now than I ever did in an office.

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about offices, lad, but I know the feeling of a heavy heart when the wind starts to howl. That night in Iceland, the waves were as high as houses and we were praying to any saint that would listen just to see the dawn. This boat is all I have left of Mary's hard work, so I'll treat her with more respect than a man treats his own kin. Now, keep that paddle moving or we'll be sitting here watching the tide go out with a leaky hull.

speaker: minh
text: I'm not slowing down, Jack, I promise. It's crazy how much more focus this takes than just staring at a screen, but I'm actually really into it. Is the mixture starting to look thick enough for you now?

speaker: lao
text: Aye, it's looking just right now, thick and dark as a bit of old tar. It's got the pull of it, like the sludge at the bottom of a deep trench. This bit of work is what'll keep her afloat, just as Mary intended when she tucked that money away for me. Now, grab the brush and let's get this spread thin across the seam before it sets.

speaker: minh
text: Got it, I'll grab the brush and get on it. It's actually pretty satisfying seeing it coat the wood like that, almost like I'm applying a layer of protection to a system. Do you have to do this every single season, or just when the wood starts to show some wear?

summary: Sam assists Jack in patching a hole in Jack's boat using a mixture of tar and pine resin. Jack reveals that he bought the vessel with savings left by Mary and that his son, Tommy, is approaching them.

scene_start: The village holds a wake at the pub; Jack takes Sam along and they meet his old mates.
beats: The old boys push cider on Sam.
One of them tells how reckless Jack was as a young man.
Sam gets asked about wife and kids and Jack covers for him.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The old boys push cider on Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Cheers for bringing me along, Jack, this place has a proper vibe compared to my local back home. These lads are absolutely relentless with the cider, though, aren't they? Is it always this much of a push to get a drink in you lot, or am I just an easy target?

speaker: lao
text: Don't you mind them, lad, they've had too much cider in 'em and they've lost their wits. They'll be digging up every old embarrassment of mine before the night is through, like the time I fell overboard in a gale off the Scilly Isles. Just keep your head down and let 'em roar, for they're good men despite the noise. You'll find they're easy enough to talk to once the stories start flowing.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, I'll just try to stay under the radar then. It's a bit like a chaotic server crash in here, just pure noise and no logic. Does anyone ever actually tell a story that isn't a complete exaggeration, or is that just the standard protocol for this pub?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't a clue what a server crash is, boy, so don't go talking nonsense like that. Most of what you hear in here is stretched a bit, like a net that's been pulled too tight. Old Bill over there will tell you he fought a shark with a wooden spoon, but I know for a fact he couldn't even catch a mackerel in a bucket. Just sit quiet and let them have their fun, and don't you go looking for sense in a room full of drunks.

speaker: minh
text: Haha, a wooden spoon against a shark, that's peak comedy right there. I think I'm starting to feel the buzz from this stuff, Jack, it's hitting me way harder than a London pint. Does Old Bill actually believe his own hype, or is he just leaning into the bit?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: One of them tells how reckless Jack was as a young man. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Old Bill's been telling that same tall tale for forty years, and he thinks it's the gospel truth. Now hush your laughing, lad, before they turn their eyes on me. They'll be bringing up how I used to take the lugger out in a swell that would make your blood run cold, just for the thrill of it. It was a foolish time, and I've lived long enough to regret more than a few of those reckless runs.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, you were a proper rebel then, weren't you? It's mental that you'd risk it all just for the rush, like some sort of high-stakes beta test with your life. Was there ever a time you actually felt scared out there, or were you just too wired to notice?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what a beta test is, boy, but I'll tell you plain that there's nothing funny about the sea. I remember a night off the coast of Iceland when the waves were as high as the masts and the wind screamed like a banshee through the rigging. My heart was thumping against my ribs like a trapped bird, and I truly thought the boat would splinter under us. There's no rush in feeling the cold grip of death on your neck, lad.

speaker: minh
text: That sounds absolutely terrifying, Jack, like a total system failure where you can't just hit restart. I can't even imagine being out there when the hardware—well, the boat—is literally about to break. Did you have anyone else on board with you during that storm, or were you completely on your own?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what you're on about with systems and hardware, lad, you're talking gibberish. I wasn't alone, for I had a crew of six hardy men with me, though we all felt like small ants in a great dark hand. We spent the whole night clinging to whatever we could, praying to the Almighty that the hull would hold. Now, keep your voice down before Bill hears you asking about the old days, for I've no desire to hear him start singing about my youthful mistakes.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets asked about wife and kids and Jack covers for him. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Sorry, Jack, I'll dial it back, I'm just feeling a bit more "connected" than usual after a few of these. It’s just wild thinking about you lot hanging on for dear life while I'm just sitting here worrying about trivial bits of code. Do you think people back then were braver, or is it just because they didn't have anything else to do?

speaker: lao
text: It wasn't about being brave, lad, it was just about needing to put food on the table for the families back home. We didn't have the luxury of choosing a different life when the nets were empty and the cupboards were bare. I remember my father taking me out in a heavy mist, and he'd just grip the tiller and tell me to keep my eyes on the swell. We did what we had to do, and we didn't spend much time thinking on whether we were heroes or fools.

speaker: minh
text: That's heavy, Jack, really heavy—it's like you were running on a hardcoded loop of survival with no option to opt out. I guess my "stress" is just a bug compared to actually starving. Did your dad ever talk about what he was thinking in those mists, or was he just as quiet as you're being now?

speaker: lao
text: My father was a man of few words, lad, and he never wasted breath on things that didn't need saying. When the mist rolled in thick as wool, he'd just sit silent at the helm, watching the swell and listening to the water against the hull. He'd only speak to tell me to watch a certain buoy or to steady my footing on the deck. He didn't talk of fear or worries, he just did the work and kept us all afloat.

speaker: minh
text: Sounds like he was just running on pure instinct, no unnecessary processing, just focus. It’s a bit mad, isn't it, how much more certain everything felt back then compared to now? Was he always that stoic, or did he ever let his guard down when things were calm?

speaker: lao
text: He was as steady as a rock, even when the sun was out and the sea was like glass. I remember one evening when the mackerel were running thick and he let out a little chuckle at a joke I made, but it was gone as quick as a puff of smoke. He'd keep his eyes on the horizon even then, always mindful of the change in the wind. Now, stop your rambling about processing and help me finish this pint before Bill starts shouting for another round.

speaker: minh
text: Right, sorry, I'll shut it. I think the cider is definitely starting to corrupt my logic modules, I'm rambling like a broken script. Is Bill actually going to shout for another round, or is he just being dramatic for the sake of it?

speaker: lao
text: Old Bill's a man who lives for the shout, so you'd best believe he'll be calling for more before the glass is even empty. He's got a voice like a foghorn and he loves nothing more than making a scene when the landlord's looking. I'm feeling a bit of a blush coming on just thinking of him starting up with those old tales of mine. Just keep your eyes on your drink, lad, and let him have his say.

summary: Jack takes Sam to a village pub wake where they encounter Jack's old acquaintances, including a man named Bill. Jack reveals that he previously worked as a sailor, once survived a storm off Iceland with a crew of six, and learned to fish from his stoic father.

scene_start: Sam gets out his phone to teach Jack to video-call his son in Plymouth.
beats: Jack keeps pressing the wrong thing and hanging up.
It works; his son asks who Sam is.
After the call Jack goes quiet, then talks about his son.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack keeps pressing the wrong thing and hanging up. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Now hold on a minute, lad, this little glass box keeps snapping shut on me every time I touch it. I'm trying to see my boy's face, but all I'm doing is making the screen go black and dark. It's a fiddly thing, more trouble than mending a torn net in a gale. I don't want to be a bother to him, but I'd give a lot just to hear his voice.

speaker: minh
text: No worries, Jack, it's probably just a glitchy touch sensitivity or the screen timeout settings being a bit rubbish. It’s not a broken build, I promise, just a bit of finicky software to navigate. Do you have Tommy's number saved in here somewhere, or do we need to input it manually?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't a clue what a build or a setting is, boy, so don't go speaking in riddles. I don't keep no numbers in this thing, just a few old pictures of Mary and the boy. I'll not be bothering him if he's busy with his work in Plymouth, for he's a grown man now. Just tell me how to make his face appear on this screen so I can see if he's eating well.

speaker: minh
text: No worries, Jack, I'll get it sorted for you. I'll just have to manually input his number since we don't have a contact list saved on here. Do you happen to know his full name or the number he uses for his mobile?

speaker: lao
text: His name is Thomas Penrose, and he'll be using the same number he's had since he left for the city. I've got it written down on a scrap of paper tucked inside my old logbook, just in case. I don't want to be a burden to him, lad, as he's got a life of his own far from the salt and the spray. Just find it for me if you can, so I can see his eyes just once.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: It works; his son asks who Sam is. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Found it, let me just fetch that logbook and input the digits. It’ll be fine, Jack, tech is basically just magic until it isn't. Here we go, the connection is loading now... oh, look, there he is!

speaker: lao
text: Lord, there he is, look at that lad's face. He looks a bit thin, like he's been working too hard and not eating enough of his greens. I'll not keep him long, for I know he's got a busy life in that big city of yours. Just seeing him makes the fire in this hearth feel a bit warmer, lad.

speaker: minh
text: He does look a bit wiped out, doesn't he? Reminds me of how my own lot look after a long week of grinding away in the city. Do you think he's actually busy, or is he just one of those lads who forgets to take a break from the screen?

speaker: lao
text: He's always been a driven soul, much like his grandad was when we were pulling nets in the freezing swells off Iceland. He gets a look in his eye when he's focused, like a man watching a storm rolling in on the horizon. I won't pester him with my chatter, for a man needs his peace to do his work proper. I'll just tell him I'm well and let him get back to his business, lad.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, Jack, my lot are pretty much the same way when they're in the zone. It's like they've got this internal drive that just won't switch off, even when they're exhausted. Does he ever actually come back down here to the coast to clear his head, or is he strictly a city boy now?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: After the call Jack goes quiet, then talks about his son. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: He comes home when the tides are right and the season's quiet, though it's not nearly as often as I'd like. I remember him as a small thing, running barefooted along the slipway and trying to catch the crabs in the rock pools. I'd give my last pint to have him sitting here by the fire more regular, but I won't be the old man pestering him to leave his life behind. It's a lonely thing, watching the moon rise over an empty house when the wind starts to howl.

speaker: minh
text: That sounds heavy, Jack, I can imagine how much you miss him. It makes me think of my own parents back in London, though they're more about constant WhatsApp pings than quiet tides. Do you ever get letters from him, or is it all just digital stuff like this?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about a WhatsApp, lad, so I'll leave that to you. He sent me a card once, a proper thick one with a picture of a mountain on it, and it sat on my mantle for many a month. It's better than nothing, I suppose, but it ain't the same as hearing his real voice or seeing him pull up a chair. I'll just let him go now before he thinks his old man is getting too sentimental.

speaker: minh
text: I'll end the call for you now, Jack, so he can get back to it. It’s a bit different from the instant gratification we get in the city, but I guess a physical card holds a bit more weight, doesn't it? Do you have many more of those old cards tucked away in your logbook?

speaker: lao
text: I've a drawer full of 'em, some from Mary and a few from the boy when he was just a nipper. I keep 'em tucked away near the spare twine and the tallow, though they've grown dusty over the years. It's a fine thing to hold a piece of paper that a loved one's hand actually touched. Go on then, shut that glass thing off and let me sit with my thoughts for a bit.

speaker: minh
text: No worries, Jack, I'll shut it down. It's a bit more soulful than the digital clutter I'm used to, having something real to hold onto. I'll leave you to it, though I can't help but think of my own folks back home.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, you head on home then, lad, and give your folks a proper word if you can. I'll just sit here a while and watch the embers die down in the grate. I remember when Mary used to write me long letters when I was out on the trawlers, and I'd read 'em till the ink faded. It's a quiet night, and I've a bit of pipe tobacco left to enjoy.

speaker: minh
text: I'll definitely give them a shout, Jack, thanks for the advice. It's a bit too quiet in here for me to just sit and stare at the fire, so I might head out for a bit of air. Do you ever get lonely out here when the storms roll in, or does the noise of the sea keep you company?

summary: Sam assists Jack in video-calling his son, Thomas Penrose, by manually inputting a phone number from Jack's logbook. During the call, Jack reveals his son lives and works in Plymouth, while Sam notes that his own family resides in London.

scene_start: A moonlit night, Jack takes Sam squid jigging off the harbour mouth.
beats: Jack shows him how to work the jig.
Sam catches his first squid and is over the moon.
They sit quietly under the moon and Jack tells about the Iceland trawlers.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack shows him how to work the jig. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: So, how does this jigging thing actually work, Jack? Is there a specific rhythm I need to keep, or is it more about the tension on the line? It feels a bit more complex than just a simple loop of code.

speaker: lao
text: I've no notion what you're on about with that code talk, lad, it sounds like gibberish to me. You just keep a steady twitch in your wrist to make the jig dance like a living thing in the dark. It's all about the feel of the pull, much like how we used to feel the heavy nets dragging deep when I was crewing the big trawlers up past Iceland. You'll learn the rhythm well enough if you keep your eyes on the water and your hands steady.

speaker: minh
text: Got it, steady twitch, like a constant refresh rate to keep the movement going. It’s a bit harder to find that rhythm than I thought, especially with my head being all over the place. Do you reckon you can actually sense the fish coming before they even hit the line?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what a refresh rate is, boy, but stop your rambling and watch the line. You can feel the change in the tide and a certain heaviness in the air when the squid are running close to the surface. I remember one night off the coast of Iceland, the swell was massive and the wind was howling, but we knew the catch was coming just by the way the boat sat in the swell. Just keep your hands quiet and let the sea tell you what's happening.

speaker: minh
text: That's mad, basically sensing the data through the boat itself. It's a lot more intuitive than just staring at a screen all day, which is probably why I'm struggling so much right now. Do the squid usually come in big schools, or is it just a bit of a random scatter?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam catches his first squid and is over the moon. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: I've no idea what data is, lad, so leave that nonsense to the city folk. They come in thick clouds if the moon is right, just like the herring used to run back when I was crewing those big trawlers up towards Iceland. Hold tight now, look at your line, there's a tugging! Lord, look at that, you've hooked a fine one, pull it up quick before it slips away!

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, I've got one! I'm pulling, I'm pulling, just don't let the line snap! This is a proper rush, Jack, way more intense than any bug I've ever had to squash at work.

speaker: lao
text: Keep your footing and don't let your heart jump out of your chest, boy, or you'll lose him. I've seen men lose much more than a fish when they got too excited during a haul. It puts me in mind of the time we were pulling up heavy nets off Iceland and the whole deck was slick with spray and scales. Just keep a steady pull and bring him alongside the boat slow.

speaker: minh
text: I'm trying, I'm trying, but my hands are shaking like mad! It's a massive rush, honestly, way more real than sitting in a swivel chair feeling like my brain is melting. Do you think it's always this much of a fight to get something good out of the water?

speaker: lao
text: It's always a scrap when the prize is worth the effort, lad. I remember hauling gear in the freezing swells off Iceland where the wind would cut right through your oilskins and the fish fought like they had a grudge against the world. You'll find that nothing worth having comes easy, whether it's a fine squid or a decent catch of mackerel. Now steady your hands and bring him in before he finds a way to break free.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: They sit quietly under the moon and Jack tells about the Iceland trawlers. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: I've got him, I think he's in! It’s mental how much energy it takes just to bring one thing up from the dark. You mentioned those Iceland trawlers earlier, were those boats massive compared to this little thing?

speaker: lao
text: Those trawlers were giants, lad, far bigger than this little boat of mine. When we were out in the North Atlantic, the deck was wide enough to walk a dozen men abreast and the waves would crash over the bow like falling mountains. I remember the steel hull groaning under the weight of the swell, and you'd feel the whole vessel shuddering deep in your bones. It was a far cry from this quiet little harbour, I'll tell you that much.

speaker: minh
text: That sounds absolutely terrifying, Jack, like being trapped in a glitchy simulation where everything's breaking at once. It’s a massive contrast to the quiet here, but honestly, the idea of something that intense makes my office job feel even more hollow. Do you ever miss the chaos of those big ships, or are you glad for the peace now?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what a glitchy simulation is, boy, so you'll have to speak plain to me. There were nights on those big ships when the gale was so fierce you couldn't tell the sky from the sea, and it'd make your blood run cold. I don't miss the fear of the dark water, but I do miss the way the whole crew worked as one man to fight the storm. Now, I'm glad for the quiet of Polmarren and the warmth of my own hearth.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, the teamwork element sounds pretty incredible. I think I'm just stuck in a loop of feeling disconnected from everything lately. Do you reckon people can actually change their entire way of life, or are we just stuck on the path we're on?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know about loops, lad, but I know a man can turn his life about if the sea or the wind calls him. I spent my best years crewing those massive trawlers up towards Iceland, thinking I'd never touch dry land for long. Then the years passed, I lost Mary, and I found myself back here in Polmarren, mending nets and living a quiet life. A man's path can shift just as sudden as a tide turning in the channel.

speaker: minh
text: That's deep, Jack, like a complete system reboot after everything's crashed. It's actually quite comforting to hear that things don't have to stay the same forever. Do you think it's harder to make that change when you're older, or is it just about having the guts to do it?

speaker: lao
text: I've no notion what a system reboot is, boy, so stop your talking in riddles. It's not about age, it's about whether you have the grit to face the wind when it's blowing against you. I was a young man with nothing but my father's lessons when I first stepped onto those massive trawlers bound for Iceland, and it took every bit of courage I had to stand my ground. Sometimes the sea just decides it's time for you to come home, and you've got to be ready to follow.

summary: Jack and Sam go squid jigging from a boat at the mouth of the harbour. Jack reveals he previously worked on large trawlers near Iceland and now lives a quiet life in Polmarren following the death of his wife, Mary, while Sam discusses his work in an office involving coding.

scene_start: The last morning, Sam is heading back to London and stops at the harbour to say goodbye to Jack.
beats: Jack wraps up some smoked mackerel for Sam.
Sam promises to come back at Christmas.
Jack tells him one thing, then turns back to his nets.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack wraps up some smoked mackerel for Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Don't be heading off on an empty belly, lad, so I've wrapped up some of this smoked mackerel for your journey. It's the same way my Mary used to pack the tins when the men went out for the long haul. You take it and find a bit of bread to go with it once you're back in that big city of yours. It'll taste better than any of that shop food you're used to.

speaker: minh
text: Cheers, Jack, that's proper legend of you. This is way better than the processed rubbish I usually grab between sprints at the office. Did you ever use any specific spices or herbs back in the day to preserve the fish, or was it just the smoking process?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't the foggiest what a sprint is, boy, so you'll have to speak plain. We mostly just used salt and the heavy smoke from the oak fires to keep the catch good for the long weeks. My father used to say a bit of sea salt and a slow smoke was all a man needed to keep his strength. Now, you get on with your travel before the tide turns against you.

speaker: minh
text: Sorry, Jack, I mean a bit of a mad rush at work—it's basically just work jargon. Salt and oak smoke sounds much more authentic than the stuff I get. Since you've done this for so long, how did you know exactly when the fish was smoked enough to be safe?

speaker: lao
text: You just watch the color of the flesh and the way the smoke clings to the skin, lad. When it turns that deep, golden hue and firm to the touch, you know it's ready for the cellar. It's a thing you feel in your bones after years of standing over the fires, much like knowing when a storm is brewing by the way the gulls act. I've spent a lifetime watching things change and fade, so I know a thing or two about timing.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam promises to come back at Christmas. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That's mental, it's like you've got a built-in algorithm for it. I'm actually thinking of making some big changes with my career soon, so I might need a proper break from the city. I'll definitely be back to visit you around Christmas to see how the fishing is going, alright?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what an algorithm is, boy, but if you're looking for peace, the sea will always be here. I'll be right here by the slipway, likely mending nets or watching the tide come in, just like I have since I was a lad. It'll be a quiet Christmas without much bustle, but the mackerel should be running well by then. Safe travels to you on that long road back to London.

speaker: minh
text: Safe travels to you too, Jack. I'll hold you to that mackerel when I'm back! Do you think the weather stays mostly calm this time of year, or should I pack something heavy-duty for the trip back?

speaker: lao
text: The wind can turn fickle as a crab in a net, so pack a heavy coat just in case. I remember a winter back when I was a lad where the frost bit so deep it cracked the very stones of the quay. It's best to be prepared for a sudden blow when you're traveling far from the coast. Best get moving now, lad, before the mist rolls in thick over the water.

speaker: minh
text: Right, I'll pack a proper coat, cheers for the heads up. It's definitely better to be safe than sorry when the weather gets glitchy like that. See you at Christmas, Jack!

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: the scene isn't over, nobody is leaving yet. Keep the conversation going.)
(Director: next in this scene: Jack tells him one thing, then turns back to his nets. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: I don't know what you mean by glitchy, lad, but the weather don't care much for your fancy words. It'll be a lonely stretch until the frost sets in, and the house feels a bit too quiet these days. I've got to get back to these nets before the light fails me completely. I'll be here working them just as I always do.

speaker: minh
text: I get you, Jack, I really do. I'll definitely keep you posted on my news, especially since I'm planning to jump ship and find something new. Take care of yourself while I'm gone, alright?

summary: Sam prepares to return to his office job in London after receiving smoked mackerel from Jack. Jack explains that he preserves fish using salt and oak smoke, a method passed down from his father and his Mary.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Afternoon on Polmarren harbour. Old Jack is mending nets when Sam, down from London, stops to say hello.
beats: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot.
Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own.
Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Alright, Jack, looks like you've got a proper system going there. How do you actually manage to mend those holes without the whole thing unravelling like a buggy piece of code? Is there a specific way you tie the knots to make them stay?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't the faintest what a buggy code is, lad, so you'll have to speak plain. You just use a shuttle and a steady hand to weave the twine back through the mesh, tying a sheet bend knot so it won't slip. It's all about the tension, much like how my father used to say a boat needs a steady keel to stay true. You've grown a bit since the last time you were down here, haven't you?

speaker: minh
text: Haha, fair enough, I'll keep it simple. I guess I've just put on a bit of weight since the last time I was here, or maybe it's just the Cornish air making me relax. Do you find you have to replace the whole net once in a while, or can you just keep patching it up indefinitely?

speaker: lao
text: You can patch a net for years if the twine is good, but eventually the sea wears it down to nothing. I remember a great net I lost near the Scillies back in '82, and it felt like losing a limb, it did. You're looking a bit more settled than when you left, lad. Is everything alright with you and that girl from the city, or is life still a bit of a struggle?

speaker: minh
text: Nah, it's all sorted with her, Jack, we've just gone our separate ways. I'm actually just on a bit of a break from the office to clear my head. Everything's decent, just taking it easy for a bit.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: It's a good thing to have a bit of quiet to clear the mind, lad. I used to find the same when the tides were heavy and the work was hard. But what brings you all the way down to Polmarren on your own, then? Most boys your age wouldn't dream of coming to a quiet place like this without a crowd of friends trailing after them.

speaker: minh
text: I just needed to get away from the constant notifications and the madness of London for a bit. It's easier to just come down here and see the sea than to deal with the grind every single day. Do you ever get that feeling where you just need to disconnect from everything?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know much about these notifications you speak of, but I know the feeling of wanting the world to just stop spinning. There were times after Mary passed when I'd sit on the quay and wish the wind would just blow the noise of the world right out to sea. Sometimes a man just needs to hear nothing but the gulls and the tide against the stones to find himself again. You look like a man with a lot on his mind, lad.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, Jack, honestly. It's just that my brain feels like it's got too many tabs open all the time, you know? I'm just trying to find a bit of a reset button before I head back to the city.

speaker: lao
text: I haven't a clue what a tab or a reset button might be, but it sounds like a heavy burden to carry. My old mate Bill used to say that a man's mind is like a cluttered hold on a trawler, and if you don't clear the old catch out, there's no room for anything new. I'll be mending this section of the net before the light fades, so sit a while if you've the time. I wonder if that city life of yours is truly what you were meant for, lad.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That's a deep way of putting it, Jack, definitely something for me to think about. I'll definitely hang about for a bit, though. Are you heading out on the boat tomorrow morning, or are you just sticking to the nets for a while?

speaker: lao
text: I'll be out on the boat at dawn to check the crab pots, provided the swell stays low. It's a quiet sort of work, just me and the salt spray, which is a far cry from the noise you're used to. I was wondering, lad, if you've any kin of your own up there in the city, or if you're just drifting through it on your own? It's a lonely thing to be far from home without a soul to call your own.

speaker: minh
text: I've got my parents and a sister up there, but they're all spread out across different parts of London. It doesn't feel as lonely as you'd think, though, especially when I've got my mates to grab a drink with. Do you find it gets a bit quiet in the cottage when the weather turns bad?

speaker: lao
text: It gets quiet enough, lad, especially when the wind starts howling through the eaves like a banshee in the night. I remember during the great storm back in '87, the house felt like it was floating in the middle of the ocean and the silence between the gusts was the heaviest thing I ever felt. I keep the fire stoked high to keep the shadows at bay, though it's no substitute for a voice in the room. It's a strange thing, having a family so far away that you only see them through a glass pane every now and then.

speaker: minh
text: That sounds pretty intense, Jack, like something straight out of a horror film. I guess having the fire going helps make it feel a bit more cozy and less lonely. Do you have to do much prep work to make sure the cottage stays watertight when those big storms roll in?

speaker: lao
text: It's no film, boy, it's just the way of the world when the Atlantic gets angry. I spend a good deal of time checking the mortar and making sure the heavy shutters are latched tight against the gale. I remember once a wave came up the slipway so high it nearly breached the kitchen door, and I spent the whole night with a bucket and a mop. You seem a quiet sort, lad, always thinking on things, so I wonder if you've a girl or a sweetheart waiting for you back in that big city?

speaker: minh
text: Nah, no one waiting for me, Jack. I'm just flying solo for a bit while I sort my head out. It's actually quite peaceful not having to check my phone for anyone's messages all the time.

speaker: lao
text: There's a certain freedom in being solo, though it can be a heavy thing to carry when the sun goes down. I remember when I first started working the deep trawlers, I thought I wanted nothing but the open sea and my own company. It took me many years and a good woman like Mary to realize that a man needs more than just his own shadow to keep him company. You've a thoughtful look about you, lad, like you're searching for something more than just a bit of peace and quiet.

summary: Sam visits Jack at Polmarren harbour to discuss net mending and his decision to take a break from his office job in London. Jack shares that he is a widower whose wife was named Mary and that he plans to check his crab pots at dawn.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Next morning, still dark, Sam goes out with Old Jack in his small boat.
beats: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out.
Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons.
They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Steady on there, lad, don't you go fighting the swell or it'll only bring it up again. Just lean your head against the gunwale and let the boat do the work, same as I had to do when I first went out at fourteen. I remember my old man watching me turn green as a sea slug on my first trip past the Lizard. Just keep your eyes on the horizon and breathe deep of the salt air.

speaker: minh
text: Safe, Jack, I'm trying my best to keep my balance. I actually wanted to get some footage of this on my phone, but the battery's completely dead. Is it always this pitch black when you head out for the pots?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about those little glass boxes or why they'd go dead on you, lad. It's always dark as a coal mine when the tide's turning and we're heading for the pots. I remember my first time out at fourteen, shivering in the dark with nothing but a dim lantern and the sound of the swell hitting the hull. You get used to the blackness once you stop fighting it.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, I'll just try to soak it in instead. It's a bit different from my usual routine, staring at a bright monitor all day. Do you use any kind of GPS or tech to find exactly where you set the pots, or is it all just memory?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't the foggiest what a monitor is, boy, so you'll have to leave that talk to the city folk. We find our way by the marks on the shore and what's etched in a man's mind, just like I did when I was a lad of fourteen. I can still see the shape of the rocks at low tide as clear as if they were sitting right here in the boat with us. It's the old way, and it's the only way that never fails when the fog rolls in thick.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That's mental, honestly, like having a built-in map in your head. I'd probably be totally lost without Google Maps or something. Since we're heading towards the pots now, is there a specific time of year when the fishing really picks up, or is it just a constant grind?

speaker: lao
