text: I don't know nothing about a Google, lad, sounds like a lot of bother to me. The crab are best when the water's cooling down in the autumn, though there's always a bit of work to be done if you want to eat. I remember my first trip out at fourteen, staring at the stars and wondering if the sea would ever let me go home. It's a constant grind, but there's a peace in it once you find your rhythm.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, it sounds proper peaceful compared to the chaos of the city. I'm gutted my phone's dead though, because I really wanted to film some of this to show my mates. What kind of gear do we need to haul the pots up once we get to the spot?

speaker: lao
text: You'll need the hauler and a good pair of gloves, lad, or the rope will strip the skin right off your hands. We'll be pulling them up steady, one by one, just like my father taught me when I was a boy of fourteen. I remember my hands being raw and bleeding that first season, but the sight of a full pot made the stinging worth it. Just keep your footing sure and watch the line as it comes over the side.

speaker: minh
text: Got it, I'll make sure I've got my gloves on so I don't end up with shredded hands. It's a bit of a shame about the phone being dead though, as I'd love to have a high-res clip of this to show my mates back in London. Do we have to pull them up manually, or is there a machine to help with the heavy lifting?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: The small winch on the deck will do the heavy lifting for us, boy, so you don't go straining your back. There's a heavy pull on the line now, so hold tight and watch the water. Look at that beast coming up, it's got a strange shape to it, unlike any mackerel or cod I've seen. I can't rightly say what kind of fish it is, but it's a queer looking thing, isn't it?

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, that is a proper weird-looking thing, Jack! I'm so gutted my phone's dead because I'd love to get a video of that for my mates. Is that something you see often around here, or is it a total anomaly?

speaker: lao
text: I've never seen one quite like that in all my years, lad, so it's a rare sight indeed. It puts me in mind of my first time out at fourteen, when we hauled up a tangled mess of old nets and a dead shark that looked just as strange. Most days it's just crabs and maybe a bit of lobster, but the sea likes to throw a curveball when you least expect it. Just mind your fingers near the winch while we get it sorted.

speaker: minh
text: I'll keep my fingers well clear of the winch, don't worry. It's actually mental, like something out of a sci-fi film or something. Do you think it's some kind of deep-sea species that's just drifted up into these shallower waters?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about them sci-fi films you're on about, boy, so don't be asking me. It could be a deep-sea thing, or just something the currents have dragged up from the dark. It reminds me of my first time out at fourteen, when we hauled up a creature so strange the whole crew sat silent for an hour. The sea keeps her own secrets, and she don't care much for our asking.

speaker: minh
text: That's deep, Jack, properly eerie. I'm still buzzing about how weird it looks, even if I can't capture it on camera. Do you think we should try and keep it for a bit to show the village, or just let it go?

speaker: lao
text: Let's bring it back to the quay and let the men at the harbour see it, lad. If it's a rare thing, it'll be the talk of Polmarren from here to Penzance by sundown. It's like that strange thing I saw when I was fourteen, a creature so odd it made the old salts stop their swearing for a moment. We'll get it in the hold and head for home.

speaker: minh
text: Sounds like a plan, let's get it sorted. I'm still gutted about my phone being dead because the footage would have gone viral on social media in seconds. Do we have enough space in the hold to keep it safe until we hit the quay?

summary: Sam and Jack head out to sea in a small boat to collect crab pots. Sam reveals he is from London and works with monitors, while Jack shares that he began fishing at age fourteen under his father's instruction.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Midday on the quay, Old Jack sells his catch and Sam lends a hand.
goal: A morning at the fish stall.
beats: A customer haggles hard over the price.
Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off.
The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A customer haggles hard over the price. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, that guy is really rinsing you on the price, isn't he? It feels like he's trying to exploit a bug in your system or something. Do you always have to deal with such heavy haggling just to move your stock?

speaker: lao
text: Don't you fret none, lad, that's just how it goes with Arthur, he's been trying to skin me for a copper since I was a boy. He thinks he's clever, but he knows as well as I do that these crabs are the finest in the cove. That's just the way of the quay, whether it's a bright summer day or a gale blowing in from the north. I've been dealing with his nonsense for forty years and I'm still standing.

speaker: minh
text: Fair play, Jack, you've definitely got the stamina for it. It's mad how much of a grind it is just to get a fair deal on the quay. Do you ever think about getting these crabs onto an app or something to reach people outside the village?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't a clue what an app is, boy, so don't be talking such nonsense to me. I've got Bill the butcher and Mrs. Tregenza from the bakery who'll be wanting their share before the sun sets anyway. We sell what we catch to the folk we know, and that's plenty enough for an old man like me. It's the hands and the salt that matter, not these strange words you're using.

speaker: minh
text: My bad, Jack, I didn't mean to sound like a total geek. I guess sticking to the locals is a much more solid way to run things without all the extra noise. Do Bill and Mrs. Tregenza come down here every single day at the same time?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Mrs. Tregenza's always here by ten for her morning catch, and Bill usually wanders down after he's finished with the meat. They're as regular as the tides, and you can set your watch by 'em. Now, hold on a minute, lad, you've given me two pence too little in that change. Ha, don't look so worried, it's just a little mistake and I've seen worse in a thick fog.

speaker: minh
text: Shit, sorry about that, Jack—my brain must be lagging today. I'll get that sorted right now. Is it usually this hectic on the quay when everyone shows up at once?

speaker: lao
text: It's always a bit of a scramble when the tide's right and the boats come in, lad. You'll see young Billy pulling his nets up just over there, and old Silas usually comes stomping down from the cliffs when the mackerel are running. It gets a proper muddle of it, with all the shouting and the heavy crates being dragged across the stone. But that's the life of the quay, and I wouldn't have it any other way.

speaker: minh
text: It sounds proper chaotic, like a massive system crash in real life. I can see why you'd prefer the old-school way if it's always this mental. Does Silas ever help you out with the heavy lifting, or does he just turn up to watch the madness?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about no system crashing, boy, you're speaking gibberish again. Old Silas is too old and creaky in his joints to be lifting anything heavier than a pipe, so he mostly just stands there leaning on his stick and grumbling about the weather. He'll tell you the wind is turning sour before the clouds even show it, though his eyes aren't what they used to be. He's more of a watcher than a worker, just like a seagull perched on a piling.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Haha, that's a mental image, Silas acting like a feathered lookout. Wait, did that woman just call me your son-in-law? I think she's taking the piss, Jack!

speaker: lao
text: That'll be Mrs. Penhaligon, and she's always been one for a bit of mischief and tall tales. She likely thinks you're a good lad and wants to see me married again, though my Mary's been gone too long for that. Don't mind her tongue, she's just got a habit of stirring the pot when the sun is high. She's been part of this village since she was a slip of a girl, and she knows everyone's business better than the priest does.

speaker: minh
text: She's a right character, isn't she? I'll just pretend I didn't hear that to save us both the awkwardness. Does she always go around making up stories like that to everyone on the quay?

speaker: lao
text: She's got a tongue like a whip and a mind for gossip that never rests, lad. Last Tuesday she told the whole village that my boat was sinking when all it was was a bit of low tide in the harbour. Even young Tom, my grandson, had to laugh when she told him I'd taken up dancing in my old age. She'll weave a yarn out of thin air just to see if she can make a man's face turn red.

speaker: minh
text: That is absolutely mental, she sounds like a proper menace! I wouldn't want to be on the receiving end of one of her "updates" if I were you. Do you think she'd ever stop talking long enough to actually help you sell any of this catch?

speaker: lao
text: She wouldn't lift a finger to help with the crates, lad, she'd sooner drop a bit of gossip than a bit of fish. She's more useful for telling the village when the weather's turning than she is for any real work on the quay. I remember when she tried to tell the postman that my son had won the lottery, and the poor man nearly fell off his bicycle. You're better off just nodding and smiling until she's moved on to the next person.

speaker: minh
text: That sounds like a proper nightmare, just constant misinformation spreading through the village. I'll definitely stick to the nodding and smiling method then. Do you think people would actually buy from you if you could get the word out to more than just the locals?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know about any more folk, lad, because I've got enough to keep me busy with the lot of 'em. Between Arthur's haggling and Mrs. Penhaligon's chatter, I've got my hands full just standing here on the stones. I remember when the big trawlers used to come in and the whole harbour would be thick with men from all over, but we've always just traded with our own. If I had more folk buying, I'd have to spend all my time talking instead of being out on the swell where it's quiet.

summary: Sam assists Jack with selling his crab catch on the quay while discussing local traders like Arthur, Bill the butcher, and Mrs. Tregenza. Jack reveals that his wife Mary is deceased, he has a grandson named Tom, and he refuses to use modern technology to sell his stock.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Evening, a storm is coming in; Sam runs down to help Jack haul the boat up the slipway.
beats: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips.
Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987.
The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Watch out, lad, that rope's slipped right through the cleat! The wind's got a wicked bite to it tonight, just like the night we lost young Billy back in eighty-seven. Grab hold of that line before the swell takes the hull against the stones. Get your weight into it, boy, or we'll be losing the whole boat to the sea.

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, Jack, that's actually terrifying! I've never seen the sea go mental like this, it's like a glitch in the system but way more real. Is the slipway always this dodgy when the weather turns?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know nothing about your systems or glitches, lad, I only know the sea don't care for man's words. The slipway's always a treacherous thing when the gale starts howling like a banshee. I seen the waves turn black and swallow everything whole during the great storm, and the sea's been just as hungry ever since. Just keep your eyes on the water and your hands on that rope, boy.

speaker: minh
text: I'm trying, Jack, but my hands are absolutely shaking! It’s proper mental out here, like something straight out of a movie. Did you actually see waves that big during that great storm you mentioned?

speaker: lao
text: I saw waves taller than the mast of a trawler, lad, and they'd come at you out of the blackness like mountains falling. I stood on the deck in eighty-seven and watched the spray fly so thick you couldn't see your own boots. It was the night we lost young Billy to the swell, and the sound of it still haunts my sleep. Don't be worrying about movies, boy, just keep your footing on these stones.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That sounds absolutely heavy, Jack, I can't even imagine being in that. It’s wild how much the sea can change in a single night. Was there anything you could even do to prepare once you saw the sky turning like that?

speaker: lao
text: You check the lashings and pray to the Lord, lad, but the sea don't listen to prayers when she's in a rage. I remember seeing the sky turn a bruised purple and knowing the wind was coming to take something. We worked like madmen to batten down the hatches, but even then, the dark water finds a way in. It's a heavy thing to realize you're nothing more than a speck on the swell once the storm truly breaks, boy.

speaker: minh
text: It’s proper terrifying, isn't it, like the whole world is just crashing down around us? I’ve spent my life staring at screens in a climate-controlled office, so this feels like a total system shock. Do you have a specific spot you always check first when the sky starts looking that bruised?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what you mean by a system shock, lad, but the sky's got its own way of telling you what's coming. I always look to the horizon where the clouds meet the swell, searching for that heavy, dark line that tells of a brewing gale. When I saw that same bruised colour back in eighty-seven, my heart sank because I knew the sea was getting ready to claim its due. I just look at the birds, boy, for if they're heading for the cliffs, you know the wind is coming to howl.

speaker: minh
text: So you basically use the birds as a sort of early warning sensor? That's actually dead clever, way more reliable than any weather app I've got on my phone. Are there any particular birds you look out for when things start getting peak?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: It's the gulls, lad, when they stop diving and start huddling low in the lee of the cliffs, you know the worst is coming. Now come on, let's get inside my cottage before the rain soaks us to the bone. I've got a bit of dried fish and a warm hearth waiting for us, so let's move quick. My old Mary always said there's no sense in catching a chill when the heavens open up.

speaker: minh
text: Safe, let's get out of this wind, I'm absolutely freezing! It's actually kind of exhilarating being in the middle of it, even if I am low-key terrified. Do you always have the fire going like this when the weather turns?

speaker: lao
text: I always keep the hearth ready, lad, for there's nothing worse than a cold bone when the wind's screaming at the door. It brings me back to the nights after the great storm when I sat here alone, staring at the embers and thinking of young Billy. I could still hear the roar of the Atlantic outside, just like it's doing now. Come on then, sit yourself by the fire and get the warmth back into your hands, boy.

speaker: minh
text: Cheers, Jack, I really need this. It’s actually mad how much more intense a real storm is compared to just seeing it on a screen. Does the house ever shake when the wind gets this loud, or is it just my nerves?

speaker: lao
text: The house will rattle in its very foundations when the gale hits the cliffs just right, lad. I remember the rafters groaning in eighty-seven like the house itself was in pain, and I sat here shivering in the dark. It wasn't just my nerves, for the wind can push a man right through a stone wall if it has the mind to. Just sit still by the heat and let the house settle, boy.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, that's proper intense, Jack. I'm sitting here feeling like the whole building's about to crash, but it's also kind of a massive rush. Do you have any stories about how you managed to stay calm when the rafters were groaning like that?

speaker: lao
text: You don't stay calm, lad, you just hold onto your memories and wait for the morning light. I spent many a night clutching my tea and thinking of Billy, wondering if he was out there in the dark water. There ain't no trick to it but sitting quiet and letting the storm do its worst. The groaning of the wood is just the house's way of talking to the wind, boy.

speaker: minh
text: That's a heavy way to live, just waiting it out in the dark. It’s a bit different from my world, where we just troubleshoot a bug and move on to the next task. Do you find it easier to sleep once the wind finally dies down?

summary: Sam and Jack work together to haul a boat up a slipway during an approaching storm. Jack reveals that he lost a person named Billy to the sea in 1987 and mentions his wife, Mary, while Sam discloses that he previously worked in a climate-controlled office staring at screens.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Stormy night, Sam stays at Jack's cottage; they sit by the fire.
beats: Jack toasts kippers for Sam.
Sam finally tells the truth about burnout and the breakup.
Jack talks about his late wife.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack toasts kippers for Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That smells incredible, Jack, properly next level. Is there a specific way you prep the kippers before they hit the fire, or is it just straight in? It's a massive upgrade from the sad microwave meals I was hacking together in London.

speaker: lao
text: You don't just toss 'em in like a fool, lad, or you'll ruin the flesh. My old man used to say you have to salt 'em just right and let 'em sit until they're firm before the smoke touches 'em. I remember a winter back in '74 when the frost was so thick we had to chip the salt out of the barrels with a hammer. If you rush the prep, you're just eating burnt skin and nothing more.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, that sounds like a proper mission just to get a snack ready. It’s wild how much patience goes into it, whereas everything back home is just instant-on or nothing. I guess it's a bit like debugging code; if you rush the initial setup, the whole thing just crashes later on.

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what you're talking about with that code business, boy, it sounds like gibberish to me. It puts me in mind of a young lad named Billy who tried to mend a torn trawl net in a hurry during a gale off the Scilly Isles. He didn't take the time to knot it true, and the whole thing split wide open the moment it hit a heavy haul. He spent the rest of the night shivering in the swell while the catch drifted right through the gaps.

speaker: minh
text: That’s heavy, Jack, I'm sorry to hear about Billy. It’s funny you say that, because I feel like I’ve been doing the same thing, just with my life instead of a net. I kept trying to force everything to work perfectly in London, but I was just letting the whole thing split open while I stared at a screen.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam finally tells the truth about burnout and the breakup. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: You look like you've got the weight of the whole Atlantic on your shoulders, lad. It reminds me of a time when my brother tried to sail a heavy lugger through the channel while his heart was torn in two over a girl in Penzance. He was so caught up in his misery that he missed the signal lights and nearly ran aground on the rocks at Land's End. A man can't keep a steady course when his mind is drifting elsewhere.

speaker: minh
text: I get that, Jack, I really do. Honestly, my head's been all over the place because of this breakup, and it's felt like I've been drifting off course for months. It's hard to focus on the logic and the data when your heart's just crashing like a bad server.

speaker: lao
text: I don't know about any servers, but I remember a skipper named Elias who lost his best mate in a sudden squall. He sat in the harbor for three days straight, staring at the tide and refusing to touch a tiller. Eventually, old Mrs. Tregenza brought him a bowl of hot stew and told him the sea wouldn't wait for his grief to pass. He finally climbed back aboard, even if his hands were shaking like a leaf in a gale.

speaker: minh
text: That's deep, Jack, it's like she gave him a hard reboot when he needed it most. I think I've been sitting in the harbor for a few months now, just staring at the tide and waiting for something to click. I'm honestly terrified that once I go back to London, I'll just be stuck in that same loop again.

speaker: lao
text: You're talking nonsense again with that reboot business, boy, but I hear what you're saying. It reminds me of a young deckhand named Pip who was terrified of heading back out to the deep water after a bad swell nearly capsized his dinghy. He sat on the quay for a whole season, convinced the sea was out to get him, until he watched the tide pull the sand right out from under his feet. He realized then that the tide don't care if you're ready or not, it just keeps coming in and going out.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack talks about his late wife. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: That's a proper reality check, I guess, the world doesn't just pause because you're struggling. It’s like the tide is this constant background process that never stops running, whether you're ready for the update or not. Does it ever get easier, Jack, or do you just get better at navigating the swells?

speaker: lao
text: I've no notion of what a background process is, lad, so speak plain if you can. It's a bit like when I first took the helm of my own boat after Mary passed, thinking I'd never find the rhythm of the waves again. I spent many a night feeling like the swell was trying to swallow me whole, until I learned to read the way the light hits the whitecaps before a storm. You don't stop the waves from coming, you just learn when to trim the sails to keep from being rolled.

speaker: minh
text: That's actually really beautiful, Jack, thanks for saying that. It's just... since the breakup, I've felt like I'm constantly being rolled by these massive waves and I can't find my footing at all. I'm scared that if I try to trim my sails, I'll just end up losing everything I've built.

speaker: lao
text: There was an old man in Mousehole who owned a fine little smack, and he was so afraid of a bit of wind that he kept his boat tied tight to the pier every single day. One night, a sudden surge came in and the ropes snapped, tossing his boat right into the jagged rocks because he hadn't even let her float free. He lost the whole vessel because he was too busy trying to hold onto it. You've got to let the boat sit in the water, lad, or the sea will just take it from you when you least expect it.

speaker: minh
text: That's a proper gut punch, Jack, but I think I get what you're saying. I've been so terrified of things breaking that I've basically been tying myself to the pier, just waiting for the surge to hit. I think I need to actually let myself float for a bit instead of just white-knuckling the ropes.

speaker: lao
text: That's the way of it, lad, and it's a hard lesson to learn. I remember a young lad named Toby who tried to carry his entire catch home in one giant, heavy basket instead of using smaller ones. He walked so stiffly, trying not to spill a single crab, that he tripped over a loose stone on the path and ended up in the mud with nothing left but broken shells. Once he started taking smaller loads, he found he could walk steady even when the ground was uneven.

speaker: minh
text: I guess I've been trying to carry the whole catch at once, trying to fix my career and my heart in one go. It’s probably better if I just focus on one small load at a time, like Toby. To be honest, Jack, I've felt pretty broken lately, like I'm just those empty shells in the mud.

speaker: lao
text: Don't go thinking you're nothing but broken shells, boy, because even a cracked shell can hold a bit of salt. I remember an old boatswain named Silas who had a leg that was ruined by a heavy crate in the old days. He spent years limping and cursing his luck, until he learned to balance his weight differently on the deck so he could still walk the lines as straight as any man. He wasn't the same as he was before the accident, but he found a new way to stand against the wind.

summary: Sam visits Jack at his cottage during a storm and discusses his recent breakup and struggles with his career in London. Jack shares stories of his past, including the death of his wife Mary and his experiences with various sailors.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) Morning after the storm, Jack's boat is holed; Sam watches him patch the hull.
beats: Jack shows Sam how to mix the tar for the patch.
Tommy runs down wanting to help and knocks over the tar pot.
Sam asks why Jack doesn't buy a new boat.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack shows Sam how to mix the tar for the patch. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Now, pay attention, lad, because you can't just slap it on like paint. You've got to mix this tar with the resin just so, or the sea'll find its way through the seam before the tide turns. This old girl's seen many a gale, but she'll hold if we do this right. My Mary, God rest her, she saved every penny she had just to see me get this boat on the water.

speaker: minh
text: That’s proper intense, Jack, looks way more complex than just patching a bug in some code. Is it basically like a physical version of a seal, just layering it to make it watertight? How long does that mixture actually take to set before you can head out again?

speaker: lao
text: I haven't a clue what you're on about with that code business, boy, so don't go muddling me head. It's more like a thick paste that needs to sit in the sun and harden till it's tough as old leather. You'll be waiting a good day or two for it to set right before we dare touch the swell. If we rushed it, the Atlantic would swallow us whole just for a laugh.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, Jack, I'll leave the tech talk out of it. It's actually kind of satisfying seeing something get fixed right in front of you, rather than just clicking buttons on a screen. Does the resin stay that tough forever, or do you have to redo the whole patch every season?

speaker: lao
text: It won't last forever, lad, and I'll be back here with the scraper come next spring. The salt and the swell eat away at everything if you let 'em, so you've got to keep a sharp eye on the seams. This boat's my pride and joy, bought with the very savings my Mary tucked away for a rainy day. I'll keep her tight and true, just as she deserves.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Tommy runs down wanting to help and knocks over the tar pot. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, watch out! Tommy, mate, careful where you're running! Jack, that's a proper mess now, did he just wipe out the whole pot of tar?

speaker: lao
text: Lord above, Tommy, watch your feet or you'll be wearing that tar for breakfast! That's a right mess he's made, and there goes a good afternoon's work down the drain. That resin cost me more than a few pence, and it's a devil to get off the quay once it's spilled. Get over here, lad, and help me fetch the sand to soak it up before it sets.

speaker: minh
text: No worries, Jack, I've got you. I'll grab some sand from the shed and bring it over straight away. It’s a bit of a nightmare, but honestly, it feels better to actually be doing something useful than just sitting around.

speaker: lao
text: That's the spirit, lad, get that sand quick before it turns to stone on the stones. It's a far better way to spend a morning than staring at nothing, I'll tell you that much. This boat is all I've got left of my Mary, so I won't have her legacy ruined by a spilled pot of tar. Once we've cleared this, we'll see if we can't get the hull back to how it ought to be.

speaker: minh
text: I've got the sand, Jack, don't you worry. It's weird, but I'm actually finding this way more rewarding than any task I've ever finished at my desk. Once we've sorted this spill, do you have a specific tool for smoothing out the seams once the patch is in?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam asks why Jack doesn't buy a new boat. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Spread that sand thick and don't be skimping, lad. Once the tar's settled, I'll use a smooth piece of driftwood to level the seams out. You're asking why I don't just go and buy a shiny new vessel from the yard in Falmouth, but this boat is more than just wood and iron to me. My Mary, God rest her, she worked her fingers to the bone to save up for this very boat, and I'll not be casting her memory aside for something new and soulless.

speaker: minh
text: I totally get that, Jack, it's about the history behind it rather than just having the latest model. There's something more real about fixing something that actually means something to you. Is that driftwood you use special, or do you just find any piece that's shaped right?

speaker: lao
text: It's just any bit of oak or pine that's been smoothed by the tides, boy. I've got a drawer in the shed full of 'em, all shaped by the sea to fit a hull just right. You can't go buying a tool like that in a shop, you have to know the wood and how it feels in your hand. My father taught me to look for the grain that won't snag the tar, and I've been doing it that way since I was a lad myself.

speaker: minh
text: That's mental, it's like you've got a custom library of tools just sitting in a drawer. It's actually pretty cool how you can just sense the right grain without needing a manual or anything. Do you find it's harder to pick the right wood for the repairs or for the actual structure of the boat?

speaker: lao
text: It's much harder to find the good timber for the structure, lad, as you can't just patch a broken rib with a bit of driftwood. You need seasoned oak that's been sitting long enough to hold its shape against the heavy swell. I remember my father once spent a whole winter hunting for the right timber to fix a mast after a blow. He'd say a boat's only as strong as the wood in its bones, and he was a right stickler for it.

speaker: minh
text: That's heavy, sounds like a massive mission just to find one piece of wood. It's wild how much thought goes into the foundation of something, like you're building the hardware from scratch. Do you have to source that oak locally, or do you have to travel pretty far to find the good stuff?

speaker: lao
text: I don't know what you mean by hardware, boy, but I know a good piece of oak when I see it. Most of the good timber comes from the old woods up towards Bodmin, though sometimes we have to wait months for a proper shipment. It's a long way to travel, but you can't build a proper hull with just anything you find lying about. This boat was bought with every penny my Mary saved up, so I'll not be using no shoddy wood on her.

speaker: minh
text: I get you, Jack, it's all about quality control if you want it to last. It's actually pretty therapeutic getting my hands dirty like this, way better than just staring at a monitor all day. Do you have to treat the oak with anything special once you've fitted it to keep the rot away?

summary: Sam observes Jack repairing a hole in his boat using a mixture of tar and resin. Jack reveals that the vessel was purchased with the savings of his late wife, Mary, and he learned boat maintenance from his father.

scene_start: (Sam's visit number 2, a few months later) The village holds a wake at the pub; Jack takes Sam along and they meet his old mates.
beats: The old boys push cider on Sam.
One of them tells how reckless Jack was as a young man.
Sam gets asked about wife and kids and Jack covers for him.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The old boys push cider on Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Cheers, Jack, this stuff is actually hitting quite hard. It's a bit different from the craft beers I usually grab back in London, isn't it? What's in this batch, is it homemade or something?

speaker: lao
text: It's just a proper local ale, lad, brewed right down the road by the cider makers. Don't mind them old goats over there, they've had a few too many and they'll be shouting about my foolishness soon enough. They'll likely start telling that tale about me and the giant squid back in '74 if we aren't careful. Just keep your glass full and ignore the noise.

speaker: minh
text: Haha, a giant squid? That sounds like some glitchy physics engine from a bad video game, Jack. Honestly, I'm feeling a bit buzzed, so I might actually start listening to these old goats. Are they always this loud when they've had a few?

speaker: lao
text: I've no idea what a glitchy engine is, boy, so don't be filling my head with such nonsense. They're always a rowdy lot once the taps start flowing, especially when old Arthur gets a hold of a pint. I'd keep your ears covered if I were you, as they'll be digging up every bit of my shame from the last fifty years. It's a heavy price to pay for a bit of quiet, listening to them lot howl.

speaker: minh
text: Fair enough, Jack, I'll keep my head down and just sip this. It's actually kind of nice, seeing everyone just... letting loose like this without checking their phones every two seconds. Does Arthur always get this rowdy, or is he just the ringleader of this whole chaotic system?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: One of them tells how reckless Jack was as a young man. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Arthur's been the loudest voice in this pub since he was a lad himself, and he'll be the first to start a ruckus. Just you wait, he's about to start on about how I used to pilot the old cutter like a man possessed through the swell. I was a reckless fool back then, thinking I could outrun any gale the Atlantic threw at me. It brings a flush to my face just thinking on the trouble I caused my father.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, outrunning a gale sounds absolutely mental, Jack. I can barely handle a slightly delayed train on the Tube without losing my mind, let alone a massive Atlantic storm. Did you actually manage to steer that thing through the waves, or was it just pure luck holding the line?

speaker: lao
text: It weren't luck, lad, it was bone-deep knowing how the boat wanted to move in a heavy sea. I remember one night off the Lizard when the waves were as tall as houses and the wind was screaming like a banshee. I had my hands white on the tiller and my heart in my throat, praying to the Almighty just to keep us upright. Now hush, here comes Arthur with that look in his eye, and I can feel the heat rising in my neck already.

speaker: minh
text: Shit, he's actually coming over here! I'll try to stay low-profile, but I'm definitely feeling the buzz from this ale now. What's he usually shouting about when he gets like that, is it all just old sea stories or does he get personal?

speaker: lao
text: He'll be shouting about the time I nearly ran the Mary-Ann right into the rocks at Mousehole because I was too busy looking for a bit of luck. He's a meddling old devil who thinks every mistake I ever made is a fine bit of entertainment for the table. Just sit still and don't let him see you laughing, or he'll turn his sights on you next. I can already see him waving his arms about like a windmill, ready to spill my secrets to the whole room.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: the scene isn't over, nobody is leaving yet. Keep the conversation going.)
(Director: next in this scene: Sam gets asked about wife and kids and Jack covers for him. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: I'm trying to stay chill, Jack, I swear, but my face is definitely starting to feel a bit hot from all this ale. He looks like he's about to launch a full-scale verbal attack on you. Does he always target the same old stories, or does he change up his script to keep things fresh?

speaker: lao
text: He's got a few favorites, but he'll swap them out just to see me turn as red as a boiled lobster. Last Christmas he spent the whole night telling everyone about the time I lost my boots in a crab pot and had to fish my way home in my bare feet. It's the same old songs, played on a different fiddle, just to keep us all on our toes. Just keep your eyes on your pint, lad, and don't give him the satisfaction of a smile.

speaker: minh
text: Bare feet in a crab pot? That’s a proper nightmare, man, I'd be absolutely losing it. I'm trying to focus on the pint, but it's hard when the atmosphere is this high-energy. Is there anyone else in here who's actually a bit more low-key, or is this whole village just one big loud server?

speaker: lao
text: I've no notion of what a server is, boy, so you'll have to speak plain. You'll find little quiet in here tonight, though Mrs. Tregenza usually keeps to herself in the corner unless there's gossip to be had. Most of these men have spent their lives shouting over the roar of the engines and the crashing surf, so they don't know how to be soft. I'm just wishing I could disappear into the floorboards before Arthur reaches our table.

speaker: minh
text: Sorry, Jack, my brain's just a bit fried from the booze and the talking. I guess it makes sense if they're used to shouting over the ocean, but man, it's a lot to process. Does Mrs. Tregenza actually know all the tea, or does she just sit there watching the chaos unfold?

speaker: lao
text: Mrs. Tregenza knows every secret whispered in this village from the moment it leaves a man's lips. She sits there like a hawk, watching us lot stumble about while she sips her gin and gathers the news. She'll know if I was being a fool with that boat long before I even admit it myself. Just keep your head down, lad, because she's got eyes like a seagull looking for scraps.

summary: Jack takes Sam to a local pub wake where they encounter rowdy villagers, including a man named Arthur and a gossip named Mrs. Tregenza. Jack reveals that he previously piloted a cutter recklessly through Atlantic storms and once nearly ran the Mary-Ann into the rocks at Mousehole.
